summary: South light at the south end of Burlington, Vermont's breakwater: wooden lights from the 1850s, a 1925 skeletal tower, a 2004 replica, and the 1876 General Butler rescue.

light.note: Focal plane about 12 ft (3.7 m) per LighthouseFriends; the station record gives 5.2 m. Characteristic (record: Fl W 4s) and range (record: 10 nm) were not checked against a current Light List.

structures.type: wooden tower at the south end
structures.note: LighthouseFriends: wooden lights on both ends in 1857; the southern light was knocked over in a storm in 1876. The nomination dates lighthouses at each end to 1886.
LighthouseFriends dates the skeletal towers to 1925.

structures.type: replica of the circa 1857 tower, steel frame clad in wood
structures.note: Built by Atlantic Mechanical of Wiscasset, Maine, on design based on photographs; activated 12 September 2004 (LighthouseFriends). The station record gives first lit 2003.

staffing.note: Last manual lighting in 1938 (LighthouseFriends); automatic lights from 1938 (nomination).

facts.agency: City of Burlington (owner and manager, per the Society's roster and LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Tower closed (LighthouseFriends). LighthouseFriends suggests viewing from the Burlington wastewater treatment facility and from excursion cruises.

events.note: Wooden lights placed on the ends of the breakwater (LighthouseFriends). The nomination gives 1886 for lighthouses at each end.
February ice floes and a northwesterly storm injured 220 ft of the south end of the breakwater (nomination).
The southern light was knocked over in a storm (LighthouseFriends).
Schooner General Butler driven onto the south end of the breakwater on 9 December 1876; five people rescued.
Lighthouses at each end, Fresnel-lens beacons replacing signal lanterns (nomination). Conflicts with the 1857 date.
Board's report: 210 feet of plank walk built to reach the South Beacon from the landing (fiscal 1891).
Bell struck by machinery, double blow every twelve seconds in thick weather, set on the south light on 21 October 1907 (LighthouseFriends).
Wooden towers replaced by skeletal towers with tank houses (LighthouseFriends).
Last manual lighting in 1938 (LighthouseFriends); automatic lights from 1938 (nomination).
Replica tower activated on 12 September 2004 (LighthouseFriends). The station record gives 2003.

wrecks.outcome: Schooner ran onto the south end of the breakwater with five people aboard; all reached the wall and were taken off in a rowboat by a Burlington man. The schooner was never raised.

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends gives the focal plane of the south light as twelve feet (3.7 m).
LighthouseFriends gives 12 September 2004 for the south light's activation. The record's 2003 is not supported by a source read here.
The Society's roster and LighthouseFriends name the City of Burlington as owner or manager. The record's agency came from OpenStreetMap.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends dates activation to 12 September 2004; the station record gives 2003 from the Light List. The story uses the 2004 ceremony and notes the record's date.
LighthouseFriends dates the first wooden lights to 1857; the nomination dates lighthouses at each end to 1886. The story gives both.

LighthouseFriends calls the light on the south end of the detached section the Middle Light; the Board's 1891 list has a South Beacon, and does not say which light it was. The story does not assign the South Beacon name to a single light.
The nomination and LighthouseFriends say marble; the Burlington Weekly Free Press says stone. The story reports both.
LighthouseFriends calls the 1876 rescuer the keeper James Wakefield; the nomination calls him a ship chandler; the newspaper gives no trade.

notes_for_editor: 1) Fact-check 2026-10-28. Source numbers match the story footnotes: 1 LighthouseFriends (ID 874); 2 NRHP nomination (NPGallery 02000711); 3 Light-House Board report for the fiscal year ended 1891, Third District (scan page 81); 4 USLHS place record and roster; 5 Burlington Weekly Free Press, 15 December 1876, p. 3 (OCR). 2) The 1891 Board report's 'South Beacon' entry (scan page 81; printed page not confirmed) gives the 210-foot plank walk. The OCR is garbled around that entry ('Arlington Breakwater South Beacon'), so confirm the page image before printing. 3) The same report lists a new light on the south end of the north extension (scan page 81), which LighthouseFriends calls the Middle Light. The report does not say which light was the South Beacon, so the story says so. 4) The keeper list is LighthouseFriends' list for both breakwater lights. The USLHS south place record lists no keepers, only two contractors (James E. Cashman and Luther Whitney, no dates). No person slugs are attached to south lines. 5) The characteristic (Fl W 4s) and range (10 nm) in the station record are not checked against a current Light List and are not printed. 6) Cargo: the nomination and LighthouseFriends say marble; the newspaper says stone. The story gives both. 7) The 1876 newspaper is OCR text with errors ('tho', 'Irom', 'Wakelield'); quotes match the OCR as it stands. The 'little or no injury' and Mr. Goodsell lines were checked against the OCR. 8) The nomination's north-section figures (364 ft, 200 ft gap) differ from its later figures (359 ft, 248 ft gap); not used. 9) Fact-check changes 2026-10-28: the rescue wording now follows the nomination's account of the schooner lifting onto the breakwater; the 'only one man was hurt' line now follows the newspaper's 'little or no injury' with Mr. Goodsell knocked senseless; feet are given with metres.
